clinicalPearls: Presents on the lower legs of middle-aged and older adults, especially women, as induration, erythema, hyperpigmentation and tenderness above the medial malleolus
Chronic disease produces the characteristic 'inverted champagne bottle' or 'bowling pin' leg, with a hard, constricted gaiter area and swelling above
It is a manifestation of chronic venous insufficiency and venous hypertension, often with associated varicosities, oedema and venous ulceration
The acute phase can mimic cellulitis with a hot, red, painful leg, but it is usually bilateral or recurrent and afebrile
Biopsy, when needed, shows a mostly lobular panniculitis with fat necrosis, septal fibrosis and lipomembranous (membranocystic) change
Duplex ultrasound helps confirm underlying venous reflux
Compression therapy is the cornerstone of treatment, alongside leg elevation, exercise and management of venous disease
reference.pathophysiology: Lipodermatosclerosis is a sclerosing panniculitis driven by chronic venous insufficiency. Sustained venous hypertension leads to capillary proliferation, leakage of fibrinogen and red cells into the dermis, and localised tissue ischaemia and hypoxia. Fibrin cuffs around capillaries, activation of leucocytes and release of proteolytic and profibrotic mediators cause progressive fat necrosis followed by fibrosis of the subcutis and dermis. Over time the affected lower leg becomes woody and constricted, and the compromised skin is prone to ulceration.
additionalInvestigations: Venous duplex ultrasound to assess reflux and exclude thrombosis
Ankle-brachial pressure index before applying compression
Skin biopsy only if the diagnosis is unclear, taken with care given poor healing
Inflammatory markers to help distinguish from cellulitis
Assessment of oedema and cardiac/renal contributors
Wound swab if an ulcer shows signs of infection
redFlags: Genuine superimposed cellulitis with fever and systemic upset
Coexisting deep vein thrombosis presenting as acute unilateral swelling
Significant peripheral arterial disease that contraindicates firm compression
Non-healing or atypical ulceration raising concern for malignancy
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic and progressive if venous hypertension is untreated, but consistent compression and management of venous disease can relieve pain, halt progression and reduce ulceration; established sclerosis and skin changes are only partially reversible.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating recurrent episodes as cellulitis with antibiotics rather than recognising venous disease
Applying compression without first excluding significant arterial insufficiency
Performing an unnecessary biopsy on a poorly healing leg
Overlooking a coexisting deep vein thrombosis in an acutely swollen leg
management: Graduated compression therapy is the mainstay, applied after the ankle-brachial pressure index has excluded significant arterial disease
Treat the underlying chronic venous insufficiency with leg elevation and duplex-guided venous intervention such as endovenous ablation for correctable reflux
Provide skin care and emollients, and manage any associated venous ulceration with appropriate dressings
Offer analgesia, and consider an anabolic agent such as stanozolol or pentoxifylline for the painful acute inflammatory phase, with appropriate monitoring
Encourage calf-muscle-pump activation through exercise and weight management to reduce venous hypertension
Distinguish the acute presentation from cellulitis, since it is usually bilateral, recurrent and afebrile, to avoid unnecessary antibiotics
Refer for specialist venous assessment where reflux or ulceration is not controlled by conservative measures
